I bought an all-in-one kit that has a 120x240 radiator and it does well enough for the code compiling I do on a daily basis. The stock fan wasn't able to keep temps below 175 degrees Fahrenheit. But I'm considering a doing a custom loop for the next rebuild of my main development machine.

Have you found a custom loop does better than an all-in-one? Were there specific parts of the loop that you feel like you can't compromise at all? The pump, radiator, resivoir, CPU block? What tips would you give to someone doing it for the first time?

I've watched many hours of video on YouTube about different types of builds, and there's a lot of differing opinions on some things like resivoir shapes, fluid additives or coloring, loop order, pump strength, and radiator size and fin density.

The things that pop into my mind immediately are as follows...

  • A larger reservoir does not always mean better cooling

  • From experience, I would suggest going with a soft tubing instead of hard tubing. While hard tubing can be more attractive the drawbacks are not worth it for me. Hard tubing hinders you ability to upgrade, makes moving your PC slightly more difficult, and adds more hassle every time you need to open up your case.
I was leaning more towards really good fans, at least a 2-fan radiator if not a 3-fan one. But the tip about the tubing was something I was on the fence on, so I do appreciate those thoughts.

I personally have not used a 3 fan radiator so I can't give you much input there. As far as the fans go I have to recommend you this video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pu7wI4Kn6sc as it seems to be SOMEWHAT relevant to what you're debating now.

It is, and it's one I seen before. I've also watched a lot of JayzTwoCents videos, specifically one where he talks about fan blade types and another where he talks about radiators. There's also another, slightly older one, where he talks about fans for radiators.

I would get a decent pump (mpc355 for a small loop, mpc655 for a large loop). You need to choose if you want to go soft-tubing or hard-tubing because the fittings are not interchangeable, soft-tubing is more flexible in terms of building and use, but hard-tubing has the aesthetic appeal.Your reservoir just needs to be big enough to be full of liquid during full operation, faster pump speed + bigger loop size = bigger reservoir. The blocks will do their job, there is not much difference, you can look into which metals are best (I recommend copper). One thing you should remember is do NOT mix metals, if you get copper blocks, get all copper blocks, this will prevent corrosion/stuff in your loop. For GPU, a full block will cool the memory along with the GPU chip. For radiators, higher fin density = higher static-pressure fans (higher noise), low fin density = low speed fans (less noise). I would just get the largest radiators you can fit, of course higher fin density will provide better cooling, but you need to decide on performance/noise. Thicker radiators (depending on fin density) will require push/pull setup (fans on both sides) so make sure you have space for that. The coolant is mostly preference, you can use dionized water with some biocide and add dyes to make your own, or buy a pre-mixed solution. Have fun!
Very good points on how to balance noise/performance and what dangers I could run into. Thanks!
